This initial mass is modest relative to the adult body size the snakes will eventually attain, but it is sufficient to sustain them through the first days of exogenous feeding. As juveniles grow and mature, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic development before reaching reproductive competence. Growth trajectories during this sub-adult phase are strongly influenced by prey availability and thermoregulatory opportunities, with individuals in productive habitats often reaching a larger body size at maturity than those in resource-limited environments. The attainment of puberty marks a critical life-history transition, after which females begin to allocate a significant portion of their acquired energy toward vitellogenesis and gestation. This timing also influences population dynamics, as the age structure of reproductive females directly affects the overall recruitment rate of the population in successive years.

For comparison, an average adult female measuring approximately 55 cm in total length typically weighs around 150 grams, illustrating the pronounced increase in mass that accompanies even modest gains in length past a certain threshold. This asymptotic size is achieved gradually, with growth rates decelerating markedly after females reach reproductive maturity. The substantial body mass attained by the largest individuals reflects both the accumulation of fat reserves necessary to fuel reproduction and the structural requirements of carrying developing offspring during gestation. Such large females are also capable of producing larger litters, thereby contributing disproportionately to population recruitment.

Reproductive output in female Common garter snakes varies considerably among individuals and populations. A typical gravid female produces approximately 12 to 24 young per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 12 to 24 young per clutch], with litter size scaling positively with maternal body size. This high fecundity is characteristic of many natricine snakes and is thought to offset relatively high rates of juvenile mortality, particularly during the first year of life. The timing of parturition is typically synchronized with peak prey availability in late summer, ensuring that neonates have access to abundant small amphibians and invertebrates when they begin foraging. This reproductive strategy, combining moderate litter sizes with multiple broods in favorable years, represents a flexible life-history tactic well suited to the variable environments this species inhabits across its broad geographic range.

When maintained under constant laboratory conditions at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Common garter snakes is approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years]. The disparity between laboratory and field longevity underscores the strong selective pressures acting on these snakes in the wild, where the probability of surviving to advanced age is low regardless of their inherent physiological capacity for long life. Males generally exhibit slightly lower survival rates than females, possibly due to increased movement and risk-taking behaviors associated with mate searching during the breeding season. The combination of a long intrinsic lifespan with relatively early sexual maturation creates a demographic structure in which even modest improvements in juvenile survival can drive rapid population growth.
